title: Inertia matching
goals: Work out the inertia of a roller or disc from its mass and size
Work out the torque needed to accelerate an inertia in a given time
Reflect a load's inertia through a gearbox, a belt or a leadscrew to the motor
Work out the load-to-motor inertia ratio and say whether it is sensible
Find the gear ratio that matches a load's inertia to the motor's
summary:
**Inertia** $J$ (kg·m²) is how hard a thing is to spin up or slow down: the rotating twin of mass. A solid cylinder or disc: $J = \tfrac{1}{2}mr^2$. Mass far from the axis counts most (it goes with radius squared).

To change its speed: $T = J\alpha$, with $\alpha = \frac{\Delta\omega}{t}$ the angular acceleration in rad/s² and $\omega = \frac{2\pi n}{60}$. Add friction and load torque on top.

Through a **gearbox** of ratio $i$ (motor turns $i$ times for each output turn), the load's inertia as the motor feels it is divided by the ratio **squared**: $J_{ref} = \frac{J_L}{i^2}$. Torque is divided by $i$ and speed multiplied by $i$, so energy matches.

A **leadscrew** of pitch $p$ (metres per turn) moving a mass $m$: $J = m\left(\frac{p}{2\pi}\right)^2$. A **belt or rack** on a pulley of radius $r$: $J = mr^2$. Add the screw's, pulleys' and coupling's own inertias.

**Inertia ratio** = reflected load inertia ÷ motor rotor inertia. Keep it modest: up to about 10:1 is common guidance, lower (3:1 to 5:1) for fast, stiff, precise moves. A high ratio means the load dominates: the motor cannot control it tightly, the axis rings and overshoots, and tuning is hard, especially through belts and couplings that stretch and twist.

The gear ratio that gives the fastest acceleration for pure inertia **matches** the reflected load to the rotor: $i = \sqrt{\frac{J_L}{J_M}}$.

resources.title: How gearbox ratio selection impacts inertia matching, servo tuning, and machine performance

sources: Hughes, A. and Drury, B.: Electric Motors and Drives, 5th edition (Newnes): inertia, gearing and matching
Siemens: SIMOTICS S-1FK7 / SINAMICS S120 configuration manual (inertia ratio guidance)
Childs, P. R. N.: Mechanical Design Engineering Handbook (Butterworth-Heinemann): leadscrews

formulas.name: Inertia of a solid cylinder or disc
formulas.says: Its mass, weighted by how far out it sits: half the mass times the radius squared for a solid round body.
formulas.example: A 30 kg roller, 100 mm across: $0.5 \times 30 \times 0.05^2 = 0.0375$ kg·m².

formulas.name: Torque to accelerate
formulas.says: Like F = ma for spinning things: torque needed is inertia times angular acceleration.

formulas.name: Angular acceleration
formulas.says: How much the speed (in rad/s) changes each second.
formulas.example: 0 to 3000 rpm (314 rad/s) in 0.2 s: 1571 rad/s².

formulas.name: Inertia reflected through a gearbox
formulas.says: Through a reduction, the motor feels the load's inertia divided by the ratio squared.
symbols: the load inertia as the motor feels it (kg·m²)

formulas.name: Inertia of a mass on a leadscrew
formulas.says: A mass moved by a screw feels to the motor like an inertia set by the distance moved per radian.
symbols: the screw's lead: distance per turn (m)
formulas.example: 50 kg on a 10 mm lead: $50 \times \left(\frac{0.01}{2\pi}\right)^2 = 0.000127$ kg·m².

formulas.name: Matching gear ratio
formulas.says: The ratio that makes the reflected load inertia equal the motor's own, which gives the fastest acceleration for a given motor torque.

bench.task: Pick one servo axis at work and work out its inertia ratio from the drawings and data sheets. Desk work only.
check: Find the motor's rotor inertia on its data sheet (often in kg·cm²: ÷ 10 000 for kg·m²)
List the load: masses, screw lead or pulley size, gear ratio
Reflect each part to the motor and add them up
Work out the ratio, and compare with how the axis behaves (does it ring or overshoot?)

cards.q: A load is driven through a 10:1 reduction gearbox. Compared with driving it directly, how big does its inertia seem to the motor?
cards.why: Reflected inertia goes down with the ratio squared: $\frac{1}{10^2} = \frac{1}{100}$. The motor turns 10 times faster, so for the same energy ($\tfrac{1}{2}J\omega^2$) the inertia it feels must be 100 times smaller.

cards.title: Inertia: mass that has to spin
cards.body:
**Inertia** $J$, in kg·m², is how hard something is to spin up or slow down: the rotating twin of mass.

It depends on the mass **and** how far out it sits. For a solid cylinder or disc:

$$J = \tfrac{1}{2}mr^2$$

$m$ is the mass in kg, $r$ the radius in **metres**. Because of the $r^2$, a big-diameter part has much more inertia than a long thin one of the same mass. Data sheets often give inertia in **kg·cm²**: divide by 10 000 for kg·m².
cards.more:
Spin a bicycle wheel: easy to start? Now imagine the same weight as a solid hub: much easier, because the mass is near the middle. A flywheel puts its mass at the rim on purpose.

Numbers: a steel roller 100 mm across and 500 mm long weighs about 31 kg. Its radius is 0.05 m: $0.5 \times 31 \times 0.0025 = 0.039$ kg·m².

Double its diameter (keeping the length) and its mass goes up four times and $r^2$ four times: sixteen times the inertia.

A hollow tube has $J = \tfrac{1}{2}m(r_o^2 + r_i^2)$, with the outer and inner radii: most of its mass is at the outside.

cards.q: A solid roller has a mass of {mass} kg and a diameter of {dia} mm. What is its inertia?
cards.why: Radius in metres (diameter ÷ 2, then ÷ 1000), squared, times half the mass. Using the diameter instead of the radius gives four times too much.

cards.title: Torque to change speed: T = Jα
cards.body:
To speed an inertia up (or slow it down) takes torque:

$$T = J\alpha$$

$\alpha$ (alpha) is the **angular acceleration** in rad/s²: how much the speed changes each second, $\alpha = \frac{\Delta\omega}{t}$, with speeds in **rad/s** ($\omega = \frac{2\pi n}{60}$).

The motor must give this **plus** the friction and the load's own torque, all through the move.
cards.more:
It is Newton's F = ma for spinning things: torque instead of force, inertia instead of mass, angular acceleration instead of acceleration.

Numbers: a load of 0.01 kg·m² from 0 to 3000 rpm in 0.2 s. 3000 rpm is $3000 \times 2\pi \div 60 = 314$ rad/s. $\alpha = 314 \div 0.2 = 1571$ rad/s². $T = 0.01 \times 1571 = 15.7$ N·m, just to accelerate it.

Halve the time and the torque doubles. That is why fast machines need big peak torque: it is the acceleration, not the running, that sizes a servo.

cards.q: A total inertia of {jt} kg·m² must go from rest to {n} rpm in {t} s. What torque does that take, ignoring friction?
cards.why: Speed in rad/s, divided by the time for α, times J.

cards.title: Through a gearbox: divide by the ratio squared
cards.body:
A reduction of $i$:1 means the motor turns $i$ times for each turn of the load. The load's inertia, as the **motor feels it**, is

$$J_{ref} = \frac{J_L}{i^2}$$

The torque the load needs is divided by $i$ at the motor; the speed is multiplied by $i$. The same applies to a **belt** drive, with the pulley ratio as $i$.

Do not forget the gearbox's and pulleys' **own** inertia: often given on their data sheets, already at the input shaft.
cards.more:
Why squared? Energy has to agree on both sides of the gearbox. The load holds $\tfrac{1}{2}J_L\omega^2$. The motor turns $i$ times faster, so its $\omega$ is $i$ times bigger, and $\omega^2$ is $i^2$ bigger. For the energy to come out the same, the inertia it sees must be $i^2$ smaller.

Numbers: a 0.5 kg·m² turntable through a 10:1 box feels like $0.5 \div 100 = 0.005$ kg·m² at the motor. Through 20:1, 0.00125.

This is the main reason servos have gearboxes: a small, fast motor can then control a large, slow load.

cards.q: A turntable of {jl} kg·m² is driven through a {r}:1 gearbox. What inertia does the motor feel from it?
cards.why: Divide by the ratio squared, not the ratio.

cards.title: Straight-line loads: screws and belts
cards.body:
A mass moving in a straight line also feels like an inertia at the motor.

- On a **leadscrew** or ball screw with a **lead** $p$ (distance per turn, in metres): $J = m\left(\frac{p}{2\pi}\right)^2$
- On a **belt**, a **rack** or a conveyor, driven by a pulley or pinion of radius $r$: $J = mr^2$

Add the screw's or pulleys' own inertia (and any gearbox in between, divided by its ratio squared).
cards.more:
The screw is a gearbox from turning to sliding. One turn ($2\pi$ radians) moves the table one lead. So per radian it moves $\frac{p}{2\pi}$, and that plays the part of a radius.

Numbers: a 50 kg table on a 10 mm lead screw. $\frac{0.01}{2\pi} = 0.00159$ m; squared, $2.53 \times 10^{-6}$; times 50: $1.27 \times 10^{-4}$ kg·m². Tiny, because a fine screw is a big reduction.

The same 50 kg on a belt with a 30 mm pulley (r = 0.015 m): $50 \times 0.015^2 = 0.011$ kg·m², nearly 90 times more. Belts are fast but reflect much more inertia, which is why belt axes often have a gearbox too.

cards.q: A {mass} kg carriage is moved by a ball screw with a {pit} mm lead. What inertia does the carriage reflect to the screw?
cards.why: Lead in metres, divided by 2π, squared, times the mass.

cards.title: The inertia ratio
cards.body:
**Inertia ratio** = the load's inertia reflected to the motor ÷ the motor's **rotor** inertia.

Guidance from servo makers: up to about **10:1** for general work, nearer **3:1 to 5:1** for fast, precise moves. Higher ratios can work with stiff mechanics and careful tuning, but:

- the load dominates: the motor struggles to control it tightly
- belts and couplings that stretch or twist let the load **ring** against the motor
- tuning gets hard: overshoot, oscillation, a lower usable gain

To bring it down: more **gearing**, a lighter load, or a motor with a **bigger rotor**.
cards.more:
Picture walking a big dog on a stretchy lead. If the dog is far heavier than you, every time it lurches the lead stretches and you are pulled about; you cannot keep it precisely at heel. A dog nearer your own weight on the same lead is easy to control.

The servo is you, the load is the dog, and the lead is the belt, coupling and gearbox's springiness.

Numbers: a load reflecting 0.003 kg·m² on a motor with a 0.0003 kg·m² rotor: 10:1, workable. Add a 2:1 belt reduction: $0.003 \div 4 = 0.00075$, now 2.5:1, much easier to tune.

Some makers offer 'high inertia' versions of their motors with heavier rotors for exactly this.

cards.q: A belt-driven servo axis rings and overshoots however it is tuned. Its inertia ratio is 40:1. Which change helps most?
options: Add a gearbox to cut the reflected inertia
Raise the position loop gain further
Fit a faster motor with the same rotor
Lengthen the belt for more give
cards.why: A gearbox divides the reflected inertia by its ratio squared: 3:1 brings 40:1 down to about 4.4:1. More gain on a badly matched axis makes the ringing worse, and a stretchier belt worsens it too.

cards.title: The matching ratio
cards.body:
For a load that is pure inertia, the gear ratio that gets it to speed **fastest** with a given motor torque is the one where the reflected load inertia **equals** the rotor's:

$$i = \sqrt{\frac{J_L}{J_M}}$$

In practice the chosen ratio also has to give the speed the load needs (the motor's top speed ÷ the ratio), so the answer is a balance between this and speed.
cards.more:
Too little gearing: the motor sees a huge load and accelerates slowly. Too much: the motor has to spin very fast, and most of its torque goes into accelerating its own rotor. In between there is a best ratio, where load and rotor share the motor's effort equally.

Numbers: a 0.5 kg·m² load and a 0.002 kg·m² rotor. $\sqrt{0.5 \div 0.002} = \sqrt{250} = 15.8$, so about 16:1.

Check the speed: if the load needs 200 rpm, 16:1 asks the motor for 3200 rpm, which a 3000 rpm motor cannot quite give. So choose 15:1, still close to the match.

cards.q: A load's inertia is {jl} kg·m² and the motor's rotor is {jm} kg·m². What gear ratio matches them? Give n, for n:1.
cards.why: Matched when the reflected load equals the rotor: $\frac{J_L}{i^2} = J_M$, so $i = \sqrt{J_L / J_M}$.
cards.hint: Set $\frac{J_L}{i^2}$ equal to the rotor's inertia and solve for i.

cards.q: A 50 kg table on a ball screw with a 10 mm lead. The screw's own inertia is 0.00010 kg·m²; the motor's rotor 0.00012 kg·m², coupled directly. What is the inertia ratio?

steps.ask: The table, reflected to the screw.
No gearbox, so that is what the motor feels. The ratio:

steps.show: Yes: well under 10:1, easy to tune.

cards.why: Reflect each part, add them, divide by the rotor. On a fine screw the screw's own inertia is often as big as the table's.

cards.q: Why does the 50 kg table add so little inertia in step 1?
cards.context: 50 kg on a 10 mm lead reflects only 0.000127 kg·m².
cards.model: A 10 mm lead screw is a big reduction: one whole turn of the motor moves the table only 10 mm. Reflected inertia goes with the square of how far the load moves per radian, here 0.0016 m, so it is very small. The motor gains mechanical advantage over the mass, exactly as through a high-ratio gearbox.
points: One turn moves the table only one lead
Reflected inertia goes with its square

cards.q: A 20 kg carriage on a belt, driven by a 40 mm pulley (each pulley 0.0004 kg·m²), through a 5:1 gearbox, to a motor with a 0.0002 kg·m² rotor. What is the inertia ratio?
cards.why: Without the gearbox it would be 44:1. The gearbox's squared effect is what makes belt axes controllable. (Strictly the idler pulley turns at the same speed as the drive pulley, so both count fully at the pulley shaft.)

cards.q: A load of {jl} kg·m² is driven through a {r}:1 gearbox by a motor with a {jm} kg·m² rotor. What is the inertia ratio? Give n, for n:1.
cards.why: Reflect the load (÷ ratio squared), then divide by the rotor.
cards.hint: Reflected load first, then ÷ the rotor's inertia.

cards.q: Checking an axis: a 1.2 kg·m² load through 12:1 to a 0.002 kg·m² rotor. One line is wrong. Which?
lines: Too high: needs a bigger gearbox or motor
cards.fix: Reflected load: $1.2 \div 12^2 = 0.0083$ kg·m², so the ratio is about 4.2:1: fine
cards.why: Inertia reflects through a gearbox by the ratio squared. Dividing by the ratio once made a good axis look badly matched. Energy check: the motor turns 12 times faster, so for the same energy its inertia must be 144 times smaller.

cards.q: A steel tube roller has a mass of {mass} kg, an outside diameter of {od} mm and an inside diameter of {id} mm. What is its inertia? Use $J = \tfrac{1}{2}m(r_o^2 + r_i^2)$.
cards.why: A tube's mass sits towards the outside, so it has more inertia than a solid roller of the same mass and outside size.
cards.hint: Both radii in metres, squared, added, times half the mass.

cards.q: What is a typical sign that an axis's inertia ratio is too high for its mechanics?
options: It overshoots and rings after each move
It runs slightly hotter at standstill
It cannot reach its rated top speed
Its encoder counts drift over time
cards.why: With a heavy load on springy belts or couplings, the motor and load oscillate against each other, so the axis overshoots and rings, and higher gains make it worse.

cards.q: A load of {jl} kg·m² is driven through a {r}:1 gearbox by a motor with a {jm} kg·m² rotor. The motor must reach {n} rpm in {t} s. What torque does the motor need for the acceleration alone?
cards.why: The motor has to accelerate its own rotor too: add it to the reflected load before using $T = J\alpha$.
cards.hint: Total inertia at the motor (reflected load + rotor), then $T = J\alpha$ at the motor's speed.

cards.q: A total inertia of {jt} kg·m² at the motor spins at {n} rpm. How much energy must be removed to stop it, in J?
cards.why: The same inertia that sets the acceleration torque sets the braking energy: $\tfrac{1}{2}J\omega^2$.

cards.q: Which reflects more inertia to the motor: 20 kg on a ball screw with a 10 mm lead, or 20 kg on a belt driven by a 50 mm pulley?
options: It depends only on the motor
cards.why: Screw: $20 \times (0.01 \div 2\pi)^2 \approx 0.00005$ kg·m². Belt: $20 \times 0.025^2 = 0.0125$ kg·m², about 250 times more. A screw is a far bigger reduction than a pulley.

cards.q: A motor data sheet gives its rotor inertia as {kgcm} kg·cm². What is that in kg·m²?
cards.why: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m² = 10 000 cm²: divide kg·cm² by 10 000.
cards.hint: How many cm² in a m²?

cards.q: A load is driven through a 5:1 gearbox. Its inertia, as the motor feels it, is…
cards.why: Divided by the ratio squared: 5² = 25.

cards.q: Load {jl} kg·m² through {r}:1, rotor {jm} kg·m². Inertia ratio (n:1)?
cards.why: Reflect the load, then divide by the rotor.

cards.q: Load {jl} kg·m², rotor {jm} kg·m². Matching ratio n?
cards.why: The square root of the load-to-rotor inertia ratio.
